headline: Four AI agents coordinating in real time outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 on enterprise coding tasks
summary: A new asynchronous message-passing layer, AgentRadio, enabled a team of AI agents to nearly double task accuracy on complex enterprise coding challenges, surpassing more advanced single models.
details: Researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced AgentRadio, an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows AI agents to coordinate in real time. This system enabled a team of four Claude Code agents to nearly double task accuracy on long-horizon enterprise coding questions, outperforming single agents running on more advanced models like Claude Opus 4.8.

The challenge in enterprise codebases lies in long-horizon tasks requiring multiple interactions and tool calls. Single-agent systems often fail due to a "coverage problem," where their initial plan becomes hard to revise as context grows, and late discoveries don't propagate effectively.

AgentRadio addresses this by allowing agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. This architecture enables mid-course corrections, preventing agents from continuing on dead-end paths until a formal review phase, which is crucial for highly interdependent subtasks.

The team benchmarked AgentRadio on SWE-Atlas QnA, a dataset of natural-language questions over live production repositories that require agents to run and execute software. A single Claude Code instance on Opus 4.6 resolved only 32.3% of tasks, while Opus 4.8 achieved 57.2%.

While distributing workload across multiple agents seems logical, codebase understanding tasks are rarely cleanly decomposable. Subtasks are highly interdependent, meaning discoveries by one agent can completely redirect another's path, necessitating real-time coordination and sharing of intermediate findings.

Existing multi-agent systems often fall short with parallel but isolated agents, or round-synchronized communication that forces agents to wait. AgentRadio's asynchronous, peer-to-peer lateral channels allow for continuous information exchange, preventing investigations from proceeding down incorrect paths.
